Old-timers say this forest was old when the hills were young. Cross the water at the River Clearing and the trees start listening, and past the Green Glade, out in the Old Woods and the Primeval Woods beyond, they do more than listen. My gran swore she watched a great oak pull up its roots by moonlight and stride off between the groves. Folk call it the Wandering Oak, and nobody cuts timber where it's passed.
Go on.
Maybe another night.

Mind you, not everything walking those woods is timber. Shepherds up by the Moon Hills tell of the Humming Widow's lullaby drifting down after dusk, and away south in the Black Mire squats the Hag, she'll trade you wonders, sure, but her bargains cost dearer than salt. And on the coldest nights, when every wolf in the forest goes quiet at once? That's the Primeval Wolf passing through, and even the bears in the Bear Cave hold their breath.
Is any of it true?
True enough that I keep salt on the sill and the fire lit. The forest gives: mushrooms, game, timber, and it takes. House rule: respect the groves, mind the mire, and be indoors by full dark.
You've gone quiet. Something on your mind?
A fine tale. Thanks for the telling.

Aye, it's our Ash. The inn's cat, gray as woodsmoke, eyes like embers, best mouser this side of the river. He slipped out three nights back and hasn't come home. Coldest winter in memory, that one. The wolves came down out of the high country thin and bold, right up to the fences, and old Tomas swore one of them looked him dead in the eye through his own window glass. Nobody much wanted watch duty after dark that season, and I don't blame them one bit. Traps came up empty three nights running, and torches only bought an hour's peace before the wolves crept back closer each time. It was the miller's wife who noticed something the rest of us had missed: the wolves never came within twenty paces of the smokehouse. Turned out the smell put their noses clean off the scent of anything worth hunting.

Funny thing, how a bit of good honest stink saved an entire village.

He didn't go back to that stretch of river again, not for trapping, not for anything, and truth be told I don't think anyone else rightly wants to either. Some tales are better left as tales, a light on the water, an old creak of oarlocks, nothing more than that so long as you keep your distance and mind your own crossing. All the same, if you ever find yourself down by that old landing after dark, I'd thank you to walk the long way round instead, just to be safe.
Did he ever find out the truth of it?

Inn Regular
You've spent enough evenings at the Village Inn's hearth that it feels like home. Loneliness and stress creep up on you a little slower now.
Feel at Home
"You know," the Inn Keeper says, "you're not a stranger here anymore. This is your table, whenever you need it."
Gift Wild Garlic
Hand over a bundle of wild garlic from your own foraging. The Inn Keeper's eyes light up.
Deliver Dried Wild Garlic
Hand over the dried wild garlic the Inn Keeper asked for.
Would you look at that. The well's finished, deep and cold and true. My father would have liked seeing it done. Thank you for lending a hand.
It's good work. You should be proud.
Mostly the village's doing, really.
I hear the river's got a proper bridge across it now. Used to be you'd take your chances fording it, or not go at all. Makes this whole valley feel a little smaller, a little friendlier.
It's saved me a soaking more than once.
Smaller and friendlier sounds right.
Actually, glad you're here. We're closing up early tonight and walking out to the well together, whole village, for a proper toast. Won't be long. Care to come, or mind the hearth while we're gone?
Wouldn't miss it.
Go on. I'll keep an eye on things here.

"To the well," he says later, cup raised against the dark, "and to everyone fool enough to help dig it." The whole village laughs and drinks. By the time the fire's died down, he's already talking about what to build next.
A fine toast.
Actually, I could use a hand with something. My dried wild garlic's run low and the stew's suffering for it. Bring me some and I'll make it worth your while.
I'll bring you some.
Maybe another time.
Still keeping an eye out for that dried wild garlic? No rush, but the stew's counting on you.
Working on it.
There you are. Sit, sit. I've been saving the good chair for whoever wandered in looking like they needed it most, and lately that's usually you.
The Professor at the Academy?

The Professor? Sharp as a tack and twice as dry. Comes down from the Academy some evenings for a bowl of stew and to grumble about students who don't read. Good company, once you get a few words out of him.
Good to know.
What do you make of the Inn Keeper down the way?
The Inn Keeper? A good soul, and a better cook than any of us give credit for. I take my supper there most evenings, it's quieter than the lecture hall, and nobody asks me to grade anything.
Good to know.
Got anything for trade?
Where were your rounds today?
How am I doing as a student?
Test me, Professor.
Any advice for a field scholar?
How did you come to teach here?
The innkeeper's cat has taken to me.
The river bridge is finished.
I had good teachers.

Stand still a moment. Six courses. Six! In all my years at this lectern nobody has taken every degree the Academy offers. Consider yourself, formally, our first Valedictorian. This purse is the endowment prize; I've been guarding it for someone worth handing it to.
Thank you, Professor.

One moment, before anything else. You've passed your first course. Do you know how few villagers ever finish one? Here, a small prize from the Academy's coffers. Put it toward your next enrollment, or don't; it's yours.
Come in, come in. Of everyone in this village, you're the only one who asks the right questions. Sit. What's on your mind?
Ah, my favorite irregular student. I was hoping you'd stop by. What shall it be today?
Spring again. The forest floor is a syllabus all its own, every seedling a footnote. What can I do for you?
A fine summer's day. I would lecture outdoors if the students wouldn't doze in the grass. What brings you?
Autumn: harvest for farmers, examinations for scholars. Both reward preparation. Yes?
Bitter out. A good season for study: the cold keeps the mind sharp and the students indoors. What do you need?
Noted, Professor.
The path today: mostly gravel and gossip, but I picked up a few useful stones. Mind the ruts by the old fencepost if you head that way.
The farmland. Good roots this time of year, if you know where the soil stays soft. The farmer thinks I'm mad, wading about the furrows with a satchel. He may be right.
Just the village square, trading pleasantries and picking up oddments. One learns more at a market stall than in some lectures, though don't quote me to my students.
The Foraging Forest. Mind the nettles. Worth every sting, though; the understory was generous today. Half my satchel came from a single clearing.
Frankly? You've yet to sit a single final. The lectern takes deposits of salt, nuggets, or coin, and I promise the hours pass faster than you fear. Come. Ignorance is curable.
Coming along well. You've a degree to your name, more than most who drift through here. Keep at it; the Academy's best shelf is reserved for those who finish all six.
You've finished everything I can teach. It's an odd feeling, being out of material. Visit anyway; colleagues are rarer than students.
Advice? Carry twine. Half of field scholarship is tying bundles. The other half is writing things down before you forget where you found them. And never eat a mushroom you can't name twice.
Go on.

I taught in Duros, once: proper halls, proper stipends, proper politics. The politics won. A travelling merchant told me of a village raising an academy out of mud and stubbornness, and I found I preferred the stubbornness.

The first winter I lectured to three farmers and a goat. The goat left. The farmers stayed; one of them built the desk you've seen me at. You ask why I stay; that desk is why. Now, enough of an old man's history.
So YOU'RE the one Ash chose. That cat used to prowl my lecture hall as if he held the deed to it. Mind he doesn't sleep on your notes; he has a scholar's instinct for the exact page you need.

The river bridge, finished at last! Do you know what a bridge is to a village like this? A thesis in timber, proof we intend to be more than a clearing with opinions. Enrollment will thank you within the season.
Very well. A question from the entrance examination. A student returns from the forest fevered, with an angry wound. Which remedy do you reach for first?
Raw spirit mushrooms, chewed slowly.
A plantain poultice, cleaned and bound.
A strong fireroot tea, piping hot.
Precisely. Clean it, draw it, bind it; the poultice does the arguing. Full marks. The Academy awards small prizes for sound fundamentals; here.
Mm. No. Your patient is now feverish AND disappointed. Review your herbals and ask me again. The examination allows retakes; the forest rarely does.

The Professor could use three nettle leaves for his herbarium presses. A scholar's errand, paid in metal.
Ah, perfect specimens, barely bruised! These go straight to the presses. Your pay, as promised. Keep an ear out; I'll have another errand within the week.

Steady. The farm carts me their grain and I send back flour, and I keep a pinch of every sack, which is how a miller stays fed. Bring me a good harvest some autumn and you'll see the stones sing.

It's young yet, but it has good bones: a well, honest neighbors, and now a roof of my own. A place worth grinding for. You built a piece of that, you know.

Ah, the one who built me this cabin, come in, mind the drying racks. The forest's been good to me: nettle by the stream, moss on the north stones, more roots than I can press in a day. It's the finest workshop I've ever kept.

Just looking in on you.

Salves, mostly: healing and soothing both, and teas for whatever the season throws at you. Dry the willow bark right and it'll take the edge off any ache. Bring me herbs I don't have to walk for and I'll always find you a fair trade.
I'll keep that in mind.

Quiet, and I like it quiet. The wolves keep their distance and the pines keep the wind off. I trained at the Academy same as you might have, but a herbalist belongs where the herbs grow, not behind a lectern. This clearing is exactly where I ought to be.
It suits you.

Funny you should say it, I've been thinking the same. The forest keeps me stocked but nobody walks all this way for a tea. If you could build one of those market stalls for the village square, I'd tend it myself between pressings. Build one and bring it to me.
I'll build it and bring it to you.

The stall's a joy: I set it up in the square each morning and walk back here at dusk. Folk who'd never brave the forest for a remedy will happily buy one over a market counter. You did me a real kindness with that. Come find me there if the cabin's empty.
Glad it's working out.

Got a story for me?
Anything you need a hand with?

Actually, since you're asking. My own store's run thin and the farm's grain hasn't come round yet this week. Bring me a wheat grain and I'll owe you one. Nothing fancy, just don't want the stones sitting idle.
I'll bring you some.
Maybe another time.
There we are. Stones'll sing again by morning. I won't forget this, you're the sort of neighbor this village needed, and didn't know it yet.
Glad to help.

A story? Ha. All right, since you built me the roof. Years back, before I ever came here, I milled in a town three valleys over. There was another miller across the river, proud man, and one harvest we made a wager: whoever ground a full cart of grain fastest by sundown kept the other's best grindstone.
And? Who won?

I did, by two full sacks. But here's the thing about a wheel wager: it isn't the arms that win it, it's the water. I'd spent the whole week before quietly clearing the leaves and silt out of my own millrace so the wheel ran free, while his was choking half-shut and he never thought to look.
Did you play fair?

Fair? I kept my own house in order and he didn't, that's all. Nothing in the wager said a word about whose race ran cleaner. Still, I'll grant you it wasn't the whole of it, and I've never quite told it straight to anyone until now.
So you admit it.
Your secret's safe with me.

He took it in good humor in the end, once his temper cooled. Told me a miller who watches his water deserves the wheel, and gave me the grindstone without another word. I've cleared my race every week since, out of respect for him as much as habit. Just don't go repeating the water part around the village, eh?
Wouldn't dream of it.
Got a story for me?
Anything you need a hand with?

If you're passing the farm rows, I've a pattern I've been dying to try, but it wants more flax than my own plot gives up in a season. Bring me a good bundle of dried flax stems and I'll show you something worth the wait.
I'll gather some for you.
Maybe another time.

Oh, this'll do nicely. Here, I sketched a wall hanging out ages ago and never had the flax to spare for a first try. The pattern's yours now, same as the idea was. Loom's always warm if you want to see it made.
Thank you, I'll treasure it.

A story. Let me think. My mother wove before me, and hers before her. The last winter she was well, she was spinning a spindle of nettle-fiber thread by the fire, thin as a hair and twice as stubborn. She said nettle punishes a lazy hand but never a patient one.
What happened to it?

She never finished it. She got too weak to hold the spindle steady, and it sat on the shelf half-spun through the whole of that last spring. I couldn't bring myself to touch it. It felt like finishing it would mean she was really gone.
Did you ever pick it up?

A full year later, on the first cold night, I finally sat down and spun the rest of it. My hands remembered hers, somehow. The thread came out even, no knots, no breaks, the whole length of it. I still don't know how, patient hand or not. I keep telling myself I made it. Truthfully I think we made it together.
What did you do with the thread?

I wove it into the hem of the shawl I wear every winter, this one, here. You'd never pick it out from the rest, and that's the point. She's a single thread running through the whole of it, holding, not breaking. So when I tell you a good thread is worth waiting a year for, you understand I mean it more than one way.
That's the finest thing I've heard in a long while.
Anything else you're short on?

Since you're forever in those woods anyway, there are three things I've never enough of on hand: billberries, springberries, and spirit mushrooms, all fresh, mind, not dried. Bring me all three together and I'll finally have what I need for something stronger than what I sell.
I'll keep an eye out for all three.
I'll see what I can do.

All three, and none of them bruised. You've got a forager's hands, whether you know it or not. Give me a day or so and I'll have something worth more than a tea for it. Here, the recipe's yours too; you've earned the knowing of it.
Happy to forage for you.
Need anything pressed for your herbarium?
As it happens, I've a standing request on the board for nettle leaves, three fresh ones, whenever you've a moment in the forest. Small thing, but my herbarium thanks you all the same.
I'll keep an eye out.

You know, this inn's always had exactly one cat. Never two, never none for long, just the one. Ash isn't the first. Before him there was an old three-legged tom named Soot, black as a cold hearth, and he picked my father the very same way Ash picked you: walked in unbidden one evening and simply decided he lived here.
What became of Soot?

One hard winter he wandered off into the Old Woods and never came back. We looked, I'll tell you, we looked for weeks. And then for two full years, not a single cat came near the place. Not a stray, not a barn kitten, nothing. It was as if the inn itself was in mourning and wouldn't take another.
And then Ash turned up?

The very week the well was finished, out he strolled from nowhere, this scruffy young thing, and made himself at home on the warm hearthstone like he'd always owned it. I've chosen to believe, half in jest and half not, that a place only earns a cat again once it's proven it deserves one. And you helped prove it.
Maybe he was just waiting for the right place to be worth it.

Well now, come in, come in. A new face in the valley is rarer than a dry spring. Sit; the fire doesn't charge. I keep this inn, and if you mean to last in these woods, you and I ought to get acquainted first.
How do things work around here?
Just warming my hands for now.

Simple enough. Minted coin is scarce out here; what the village trusts is salt and metal. Salt, nuggets, coins: all of it spends. Leave a deposit with me and I'll keep you an account, meals and a warm bed drawn against it at fair rates. The Academy across the way runs the same: the Professor draws tuition from a lectern account for his courses. Earn, deposit, spend: that's the whole economy.
Anything around here I could help with?
I'll think it over.

Now that you ask, this village dreams bigger than its hands. A proper cottage for a miller: there's a man who'd grind grain for the whole valley if he had a roof over his stones. Another for a weaver, so we stop hauling every bolt of cloth in by cart. And a Village Hall, so the place finally has a heart to gather in. Help raise them, and you'll find this village doesn't forget its friends.
Count me in.

Ha! I knew I liked you. The plans are yours to study whenever you're ready, no rush; the village has waited this long. Ask around, lend a hand where you can, and watch this valley wake up. My door's always open: a meal, a bed, or a look through the pantry.
(Shake his hand)

The short of it: salt, nuggets, and coins are what spend here. Leave a deposit with me and your meals and bed draw against it; the Professor's lectern takes tuition the same way. And the projects: the Miller's Cottage, the Weaver's Cottage, and the Village Hall. The plans are in your journal; the hope is all ours.
Thanks for the refresher.
Remind me how the village works.

Hm? Ah, forgive me, I don't lecture strangers. In this valley introductions come first: present yourself to the Keeper at the Inn, let him show you how the village works. Once you're acquainted, my door, and my syllabus, will be open to you.
I'll go and introduce myself.

There you are! I'd have sworn we'd met before you ever walked in, word travels, and I already think of you as one of ours. Save the two of us the formal introductions, then: this inn is yours to use, meals and a bed both, the village's projects are open for the helping, and the Academy across the way will take you as a student any day you like. Ask around and settle in.
Good to finally meet you properly.

I'll see what she can spare.

Grinding powders kicks up more dust than you'd think, gets in the eyes, the nose, everywhere. If the Weaver can spare a length of cloth, I could sew myself a proper mask instead of tying a rag over my face like some bandit.
I'll pass that along.

Good weave, tight enough to keep the worst of the dust out. Tell the Weaver her cloth's finally doing honest work for someone other than herself. Here, the pattern's yours, in case you've a dusty errand of your own someday.
I'll bring you both.
I'll see what I can find.
Since you're asking, I could use charcoal and a good handful of dried heather flowers. Grind them right and you get a pigment worth more than the sum of its parts, dyes, paints, all sorts of uses.
Glad to help.
Good char, good flowers, no waste in either. Grind them together and you've got yourself a proper pigment. Take the trick, I've no use hoarding it.
Could the Weaver help with your dust problem?
What about powders and dyes?

Give Charcoal

Give Cloth

Give Dried Heather Flowers
I'll see what he's got milled.
I've a mind to set a proper baking day, but I'm short on milled flour. The Miller's got a mill sitting idle half the week, if you'd bring me some of what he grinds, wheat or rye, either does.
I'll pass that along.

Good fine grind, the Miller knows his stones. Baking day's on for certain now. Tell him the whole Inn will smell like bread by supper, that ought to please him. Here, a plate pattern for the trouble, freshly painted to match the occasion.
I'll see what she's got.

Between you and me, some of my regulars overdo it on brew night and I'm tired of hearing about it the morning after. The Apothecary's herb paste settles a stomach better than anything I've tried. Bring me some and I'll keep it behind the bar.
I'll pass that along.

That'll settle a few stomachs come morning. Tell the Apothecary the whole common room owes her a favor she'll never collect on. Here, a burner pattern for the trouble, might as well have something nice for the bar too.
I'll bring you a stew.
Maybe another time.
Truth told, the pot's been lonely lately, same broth every night wears thin. Bring me a hot cooked stew and I'll dish it up proper, might even earn you a keepsake for the trouble.
I'll bring you some ale.
Maybe another time.
Brew night's coming and my own stock's run dry. Bring me a beer or ale and I'll make sure it's poured right, on the house even, once or twice.
I'll bring you a wine.
Maybe another time.
For the top shelf, mind, not the common stock, I'd like a wine or a second brew, something worth setting aside for a good occasion. Bring me one and I'll make it worth your while.
I'll bring you some dried foragables.
Maybe another time.
Winter's the hardest stretch for a pantry. Bring me some dried mushrooms or dried berries, whatever you've got put by, and I'll square us up proper come the thaw.
Glad the pot's happy again.

Now that's a proper stew, thick and hearty, the kind that sticks to a traveler's ribs on a cold night. The whole common room will smell of it by supper, and I expect a crowd once word gets around. Here, a painted bowl to serve it in, real color to it instead of plain clay, the least the pot deserves after being neglected so long.
I'll drink to that.

Brew night's saved, and just in time too, half the regulars were already grumbling about a dry bar before you walked in. Here's a painted cup to pour it in, better than the chipped ones we've been making do with since my father's day. Cheers, when you've a moment to sit, you've more than earned the first pour.
Save me a glass when it does.

Now that's a top-shelf pour if I ever saw one, the kind I'll be saving for someone's wedding toast or the day the Village Hall finally got its roof. Here's a painted vase to keep it in until the right occasion comes along, and around here, one always does sooner or later. You've got a good eye for quality, I'll say that for you.
Here's hoping for plenty more.

Now the pantry's set for the worst of it, shelves packed tight enough that I won't be lying awake fretting over the deep frost this year. Here, a glazed plate, tougher than the plain clay, fired twice over so it won't crack the first time someone sets it down too hard. Ought to last through however many winters this Inn has left in it, and I mean to see quite a few more of them yet.
Rough mornings after brew night?
Any baking day coming up?
The pot's been quiet lately.
Any brew night planned?
What's for the top shelf?
How's the winter pantry?

I'll bring you some leather.
Maybe another time.
Truth be told, the belts on the grindstone are worn thin as paper. Bring me some hides, small leather will do fine, and I can patch them up proper instead of praying every morning.
I'll bring you some planks.
Maybe another time.
One more thing, since you're clearly the helpful sort. My workbench is missing a good few planks, don't suppose you've got any spare from that sawmill of yours?
Glad it helped.
Now that's a proper patch job. Stones'll turn smooth as a millpond now. Here, I've been meaning to put up a hunter's platform out past the fields, figured you'd want the plans more than I would.
Happy to help.
Perfect, just what the bench needed. You've a good eye for craft, you know. Here's something for the trouble, an old stonecutting trick my father showed me. Might come in handy for flooring.
Need anything for the mill?
Anything else you're short on?

I'll see if she has one to spare.

Winter fieldwork is a misery without the right coat, and I hear the Weaver's cut a fine one lately. If you could bring me one of her cloth coats, I'd finally survey properly instead of shivering through it.
I'll pass that along, Professor.

Warm as promised, good stitching too. Tell the Weaver a scholar's gratitude keeps him from freezing in a ditch this winter. Here, a vest pattern, quilted the same way, in case you ever need one yourself.
I'll bring you some clay.
Maybe another time.

Ah, yes! A ruin out past the old tree line, I surveyed it years ago, half-collapsed even then. I've always meant to reconstruct it in miniature. Bring me clay and I'll finally have the material to try.
I'll bring you some metal nuggets.
Maybe another time.

There's an old legend the villagers used to tell, a dragon in the hills, more metaphor than beast, I suspect, but a fine subject for a cast figure all the same. Bring me some metal nuggets and I'll see what I can make of it.
I'll bring you bones or antler.
Maybe another time.

One more project, if you'll indulge me. I've been reconstructing an old armor style from bone and antler, lamellar work, older than anything smithed. Bring me bones or antler and I'll show you how it was done.
Happy to humor you, Professor.

Marvelous, good workable clay, no grit or shale in it at all. I've spent the evening sketching the castle from memory, towers and all, and I think I've finally got the proportions of that collapsed east wall right after eleven years of guessing. Here, the figurine pattern is yours. It's the least I can offer for humoring an old scholar's nostalgia, and honestly the least of what you've earned for it.
A fine lesson, Professor.

Good weight to these, enough to cast properly without the metal thinning out mid-pour. Here's the dragon figurine pattern, legend cast in clay and metal same as the old villagers must have imagined it, more shape than scale, more shadow than beast. Might teach the village children a thing or two about where stories come from, and maybe teach the rest of us that a good tale doesn't need to be true to be worth keeping.
I'll wear it with pride, Professor.

Exactly the material I needed, clean and dry, no rot in it to weaken the lacing. Here's the reconstruction, bone lamellar, laced the old way, plate over plate the way it was worn generations before anyone in this valley learned to smelt. Wear it and you're carrying a piece of scholarship as much as armor, and one fewer forgotten technique in the world besides.
Anything you need for the field?
You mentioned a ruin once?
Something cast from legend?
You mentioned historical armor?

I'll see what she's pressing.

I heard the Apothecary's finally pressing pigment worth using. If you can get me two batches, different shades, I've got a pattern that wants three colors instead of one. Worth the extra trip, I promise you.
I'll pass that along.
Three colors, just like that. The Apothecary always did have a good eye for a shade, better than mine, if I'm honest. Here, the tricolor pattern's yours, tell her I said her powders made it possible.
I'll bring you some cloth.
Maybe another time.
Since you asked, bring me a length of cloth you've made yourself, off your own loom or someone else's, I don't mind. I want to see what hands other than mine can do with warp and weft.
I'll bring you a scarf.
Maybe another time.
Bring me a cloth scarf, one you've sewn, not one you've bought off some peddler. I want to see if you've been paying attention to how I put a seam together.
I'll bring you a bundle.
Maybe another time.
Winter's coming and my own fiber stores are thin. Bring me a bundle of wool or fiber and I'll show you something to wear under everything else, warmest trick I know.
I'll bring you a large cloth.
Maybe another time.
I've had my eye on a full coat pattern, but it wants a large piece of cloth to work with, more than a scarf, more than a shirt. Bring me one and I'll cut it for you myself.
I'll bring you some large leather.
Maybe another time.
Leather's not my usual trade, but I know what to do with a large piece of it. Bring me one and I'll cut you an apron, the kind that saves your clothes from every spark and spill.
I'll bring you some leather.
Maybe another time.
One more, and then I'll leave your errands be for a while. Bring me a small piece of leather and I'll show you how to make sandals that won't fall apart the first time you cross a river.
Glad it's useful.
Now that's honest work, even weave, tight edges. You've got the hands for this, whether you know it or not. Here, I sketched a wall hanging pattern that wants exactly this kind of cloth. It's yours.
It's a fine pattern.

Look at that seam, hardly a pucker in it. You have been paying attention. Here, a hood-and-cape pattern I've been saving, a chaperon, sturdy enough for real work and sharp enough for the village square.
I'll be glad of them come winter.
Plenty here for a proper undergarment. Long johns, snug at the ankle and the wrist, keep the wind from ever finding skin. My mother swore by them and so will you.
I'll wear it proudly.
That's plenty of cloth, good weight to it too. Here's the coat pattern, full-length, warm as a hearth. Wear it well.
That'll save my clothes.
Good hide, thick enough to matter. Here's the apron pattern, worth its weight the first time a spark jumps off a fire and lands somewhere you'd rather it hadn't.
You've kept me busy, and I'm grateful for it.
Small piece, but the right size for a good sole. Here's the sandal pattern, laced tight, won't slip off in the mud or the shallows. That's the last errand I've got for now, and I mean it this time.
Have you heard about the Apothecary's pigments?
Show me your weave?
Want to see my work?
Need any wool or fiber?
Anything else you're working toward?
Got another project in mind?
One more thing for the loom?

Architecture, passed with a design I'll admit I stole a diagram from for next term's lecture. Water doesn't forgive a bad angle the way earth does, but you found the right one. With Water-Driven Infrastructure installed, a water-driven sawmill and grinding mill are within your skill now, real ones, not the toy models I sketch on the board, and with a Metallurgy degree beside it you'll be casting your own forge fittings before the season turns.

Armorer, passed, and passed properly, no student of mine gets a breastplate pattern without proving they understand why the rivets go where they go. Copper will do in a pinch, but iron will actually keep you alive out past the tree line, helm, greaves, gauntlets, the full set is yours to make now. I'd rather you never need it. I'd rather you have it anyway.

You passed Fishing, and unlike most of my courses this one I actually enjoy grading, mostly because it involves an afternoon by the water instead of a stack of essays. The iron fittings for a proper rod are yours to build now, sturdier than anything whittled from green wood. My uncle's mythical river monster is still out there uncaught, incidentally, should you fancy a rematch on his behalf.

Herbalism, passed! That's the course I'm proudest to teach, truth be told, plants don't lecture back and neither do the students who love them. You've earned the plans for a proper apothecary's cabin now, and the knowledge to mix a real healing draught rather than just crushing leaves and hoping. Go build something with it. The forest's given you enough of itself; it's time you gave a little back.

Medicine, of all courses, is the one I can't fully teach from a lectern, and you passed it anyway. Most of it is watching someone shiver through a fever and knowing which of your remedies actually helps and which just makes you feel useful. You'll carry that instinct with you now whether you're tending yourself or anyone fool enough to get hurt near you. Don't let it go quiet from disuse.

Passed, and properly, not a squeak of luck in it. Metallurgy is the course that weeds out the impatient, half my students give up the moment the ore refuses to cooperate. You didn't. You've heard, then, the Apothecary's Cabin stands finished. I taught that woman her Herbalism same as I'm teaching you, and now she's the one mixing draughts instead of me lecturing about them. There's a particular satisfaction in watching a student outgrow the lectern entirely. Do visit her stall if you haven't; between the two of us this village is dangerously well medicated.

The Village Hall, up at last. I stopped by to see it and found myself lecturing the notice board out of old habit before I caught myself. It's a strange thing, watching a settlement decide it's permanent enough to need a civic building. Ten years ago this was a clearing with a fire pit and my own stubborn refusal to leave. Now it has a Hall. Write that down somewhere, it's the sort of thing histories forget to mention.

Wonderful, truly. I've had that ruin's floor plan sketched on the same scrap of parchment for eleven years now, waiting on someone patient enough to indulge me. Don't rush the clay-gathering on my account, but I'll admit I'll be watching the door a little more eagerly than usual until you're back.

Good, good. Every village needs a monster in its hills, it gives the children something to be brave about and the adults something to blame the weather on. Whether the dragon was ever real hardly matters to the casting, metal doesn't care for the difference between history and a good story anyway.

Excellent. Most smiths won't touch bone work, too slow, not enough profit in it, but there's a reason it kept people alive for longer than metal's been common in these hills. I want to see the technique survive somewhere other than my own notes before I'm too old to demonstrate the lacing myself.

We've got ourselves a Village Hall now, notice board and all. Half the village crowded round it the first morning just to watch the paint dry, myself included, I'll admit. My father used to say a settlement isn't really a village until it has somewhere to argue about its own business out loud instead of over ale at my bar. Suppose that makes us official now.
Your bar's argument monopoly is over, then.

Did you hear? The miller's got a proper roof over his head at last, instead of sleeping next to that wheel of his like it might wander off in the night. Known the man twenty years and I don't think I've ever seen him build anything for himself before, always some neighbor's fence or someone else's barn first. Glad to see him finally spend the effort on his own walls.
Well earned, from what I hear of him.

The stall's turning a real profit these days, and everyone from the miller to the market vendor keeps telling me it's because word finally got around about this place. Every cottage, every well bucket, every fool commission the Professor's students dragged back from the hills, it all adds up to something. I didn't think I'd live to see this valley become a place worth writing home about, but here we are. Drinks are on the house tonight, don't argue with me about it.
I certainly won't argue with free drinks.

Somewhere along the way this stopped feeling like a handful of buildings and started feeling like a village people actually talk about. Travelers passing through ask after us by name now, instead of just squinting at the map wondering if there's anything worth the detour. Halfway to somewhere, I'd say, and I mean to see the rest of it built before I'm too old to pour the celebration ale myself.
You've built something worth talking about.

The weaver's cottage went up too, did you see it on your way in? She hung a length of her own cloth over the doorway for a curtain before the paint had even dried, couldn't wait a single day to make the place hers. Between her and the miller both settling proper, this village is starting to look less like a rest stop and more like somewhere people actually mean to stay.
It's coming together nicely.

Bless you, truly. A man can only eat the same thin broth so many nights running before he starts dreaming about it. Take your time, mind, I'd rather wait a week for a proper stew than eat a rushed one tonight.
I'll bring you the best I've got.

Good, good, brew night without proper ale is just a room full of disappointed regulars, and I'd rather not test how disappointed they can get. Bring it when you're ready, no rush, though if you happen to pass by on a brew night itself I won't turn away an early delivery.
I'll have it here in time.

Now you're talking. I've been saving the good glassware for exactly this occasion, dust and all, and it's high time I had something worth pouring into it. Don't skimp on the quality, either, my regulars have opinions and they are not shy about sharing them.
Only the good stuff, I promise.

Much obliged. Winter's got a way of catching everyone off guard even when we all know it's coming, same as it does every single year. My mother used to say a full pantry in autumn is worth more than gold come the deep frost, and she was rarely wrong about that sort of thing.
I'll make sure the pantry's stocked.

Hm. The builder. Word has come round to the mill, and none of it kind. I'll grind your grain and take my pinch, same as for anyone, but I won't stand about talking while the stones run. Put right whatever you've put wrong, and we'll talk like neighbors again.
I'll put it right.
Fair enough.

You. I've nothing to say to you, and I'd sooner you said nothing to me. The village has made up its mind, and I'm not about to argue with the village. My door isn't barred, mind. That's all the welcome there is.
Understood.
I'll go.

Oh. It's you. Come in, then, mind the draught. I've heard things. I don't know what's true and I don't want to ask. The loom wants my hands, and I think I'd rather it had them than a conversation. Perhaps when it has all blown over.
It will blow over.
I'll leave you to it.
Please don't stay. I don't want any trouble, and I don't think you do either. I'll sell you what I always have, and I'll keep my eyes on my work. That is the most I can do.
I mean no harm.
I'll go.

Ah. The cabin-builder. The forest talks, you know, and lately it has had a good deal to say about you. I won't turn you out: sick is sick, and I keep no grudges in my racks. But my tonics leave my hands and my confidences stay in them, and you'll find the second thin for now.
Fair enough.
I'll earn it back.
Mind the racks and keep your hands to yourself. I've heard what the village says of you, and I've no wish to test it. I'll weigh out what you ask for and nothing more. Keep it short.
I'll be quick.
I'll go.

Evening. The fire's lit and the stew's on, same as ever, but I'll be plain with you: I've heard what's being said, and it's sitting in my common room with us. I'll serve you. I won't sit and gossip. Mend what you've bent, and we'll see about the good chair again.
Fair enough.

I know who you are, and so does everyone under this roof. Nobody has turned you out, because an inn is an inn, but don't mistake that for a welcome. Take what you've paid for, keep your voice down, and don't linger. That's all I've got for you.
I'll be on my way.

Hm. The scholar's life is a cloistered one, but even here the village's talk finds its way in. I've heard what is said of you. A hypothesis, nothing more, and I hold my lectures until the evidence settles. What is it you need?
May I ask something?
I'll let you work.
Word travels, even to a quiet corner like this one, and what it says of you is not flattering. I shall answer what I must and no more. State your business plainly.
My business is simple.
I'll leave you in peace.
Give Rare Herb
A rare herb for her drying racks: a silverwort blossom or hollow sage, or a dried ginseng, reishi or hemp flower from Herbs & Fungi. She keeps it, and it warms her to you. One gift a day.

Wait, builder, before you go. I've been meaning to put this in your hands. A sack of the first flour off the stones this morning, ground fine, and I kept no pinch back. Half the village trades with me, but you raised the roof over these stones and you've been a friend to the mill ever since. Bake something good with it.
Thank you, Miller.

Hold still a moment. I finished this on the loom last night and I meant it for you: a scarf, dyed the soft grey of a charcoal wash. I'll tell you straight, it won't keep the cold off any better than plain cloth, but I wanted you to have something of mine to wear. A good thread is worth a long wait, and so is a good neighbor.
It's lovely. Thank you.

Come in, mind the racks. I've set something aside for you: the strongest draught I know how to brew, two days over the kettle. I don't hand these out, but you've brought me herbs from the deep woods and dealt fairly with me every time. Keep it for the day you truly need it.
I'll keep it safe.

Rock Wall

Collapsed Tunnel

Hire Log Splitting: Hand Over a Log

Hand the Miller a Log Piece to split. Give him four, then pay 2 Salt: he splits them into twelve Firewood (three each, the same as you would) and has them waiting in his cottage the next day. One chore at a time. The Firewood comes back at the lowest Quality of the logs you handed over.
Hire Log Splitting: Pay a Salt

Pay the Miller a Salt toward splitting your four logs. Two Salt starts the chore, and he has the Firewood ready in his cottage the next day. Open in winter too: he mints nothing, he only does the splitting.
Your logs are split: twelve Firewood are waiting in the Miller's cottage.

Hire an Escort: Pay a Salt

Pay the Watch a Salt and a guard sees you across the hunting grounds for about six hours: Hunter's Crossing, Pine Trail, Highland Pines and Stillwater Meadow turn predators back while it lasts. It ends when you walk back into the village. One escort at a time. Offered only while the Captain has no suspicion of you beyond his usual; while he suspects you, a Salt is a bribe instead.
Slip a Bribe: a Salt

Press a Salt into the Captain's hand. Offered only while he suspects you more than usual: his suspicion eases, though never below what he carries on a quiet day, and it does nothing about your crime. While he does not suspect you, a Salt hires an escort instead.
Slip a Bribe
Press a metal nugget into the Captain's hand. His suspicion of you eases, though never below what he carries on a quiet day, and it does nothing about your crime.
Town Watch Escort

Hidden countdown (0 to 24 ticks, about six hours) after paying the Town Watch for an escort. While it is above 0 and you stand on Hunter's Crossing, Pine Trail, Highland Pines or Stillwater Meadow, predators are turned back. It wears off by itself, and clears when you walk back into the village.
